If you're using Apple Watch with fitness equipment, GymKit should be on your radar. It's the best way for Apple Watch to exchange workout data with fitness machines like treadmills or ellipticals, producing results that are more accurate than either device could manage on its own.

Apple introduced GymKit back in 2017 with watchOS 4, but supported equipment has remained surprisingly hard to find. The good news is that nearly a decade later, you no longer need to spend around $15,000 on a GymKit-compatible treadmill.

Instead, you can now find a quality home treadmill with Apple Watch support for around $1,000. I spent the past summer testing the BowFlex T6 treadmill, and its combination of GymKit support, approachable pricing, and dial-based controls makes it easy to recommend.

Why Apple GymKit is so good

GymKit provides a bidirectional connection between Apple Watch and supported treadmills, ellipticals, stair climbers, and indoor bikes.

Without GymKit, a cardio machine knows your pace and distance, but needs extra hardware to measure heart rate. Apple Watch tracks heart rate but has to rely on the motion of your wrist to estimate treadmill distance and speed.

GymKit lets each device fill in the other's gaps. Apple Watch sends heart rate data to the machine, and the machine sends its directly measured workout data back to Apple Watch.

Johnson Health Tech product development director Anthony Winge told 9to5Mac that calories, speed, distance, pace, time, incline, and heart rate can sync in real time between the treadmill and Apple Watch, producing a more unified and more accurate record in the Fitness app.

My experience with the BowFlex T6 and GymKit

The pairing process is deliberately simple, but what impressed me was how flexible the workflow is. You can connect your Apple Watch before you start, but you aren't required to follow a strict sequence.

For example, I can start a workout on the T6 console, let the belt begin moving, and then hold my Apple Watch near the NFC reader to confirm the connection. Being able to pair after starting caught me off guard. For that reason, starting on the treadmill first and adding Apple Watch later felt more natural.

Once connected, Apple Watch offers four GymKit workout options: Indoor Walk, Indoor Run, Time to Walk, and Time to Run. The first two are the standard Apple Watch workout experience; the latter two let Apple Fitness+ subscribers pair the treadmill's GymKit data with Apple's audio-guided workouts.

After pairing, the treadmill and Apple Watch stay connected. Pause, resume, or end the workout on either side, and the other side updates in sync.

During exercise, your heart rate is displayed on the treadmill's console. As Winge noted, this is especially useful for zone training, because you can monitor your heart rate without constantly checking your wrist or gripping the metal sensors on the machine.

BowFlex has added GymKit across its current T6, T9, and T16 treadmill lineup. So you don't have to buy the most expensive model to get the feature.

iOS 27 brings GymKit to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3

Starting with iOS 27, GymKit no longer requires Apple Watch. You can connect an iPhone to supported equipment and use AirPods Pro 3 as the heart rate source. I tried this experience with the BowFlex T6, and it's essentially the Apple Watch GymKit experience without wearing the watch.

Separately, watchOS 27 improves the accuracy of wrist-based distance estimates for indoor walk and run. It helps when GymKit isn't available, but connecting directly to the treadmill is still the most accurate option.

Why GymKit has always been so hard to find

The biggest problem with GymKit has always been availability.

Supported machines initially showed up only at premium gyms in major cities. The lineup has since expanded to more locations in more regions, including some Planet Fitness locations, but support is still far from widespread. Even at a participating gym, only some of the equipment may support GymKit.

Finding GymKit-capable equipment for a home gym has been even harder. When I last checked in 2020, the cheapest supported Technogym treadmill was nearly $14,000. Reasonable for a high-end commercial facility, but out of reach for most households.

At the time, I hoped GymKit treadmills would eventually land in the $1,000 to $1,500 range. The BowFlex T6 sits squarely in that bracket.

BowFlex T6 brings GymKit home

The BowFlex T6 treadmill is priced at $999 (originally $1,299).

For a fully featured home treadmill, that price is still normal — roughly a tenth of what GymKit-equipped models cost last time I looked.

The T6 also skips the costly built-in touchscreen design in favor of a simple, direct console and an adjustable media rack for your own iPad, tablet, or phone. That way you can pick your own workout platform rather than being locked into a single service.

You can use Apple Fitness+ (via Apple One Premier), Peloton, Zwift, or BowFlex's optional JRNY subscription platform. Your device connects through the T6's built-in Bluetooth speakers, while the console keeps showing the workout metrics you need.

The treadmill itself doesn't require a subscription. In an era when many connected fitness machines demand an extra monthly fee to unlock their best features, that distinction matters.

The dial controls are a surprise highlight

Beyond GymKit and the approachable price, my favorite feature is the way the BowFlex T6 handles speed and incline changes.

Instead of endlessly tapping arrow buttons to make adjustments, the treadmill handles have dials you twist. The dial on the right adjusts speed, the dial on the left adjusts incline. Making real-time changes mid-workout felt much faster and more natural to me.

BowFlex pairs these QuickDial controls with what they call MaxReact drive system, which reacts quickly when you turn the speed or incline dials. The control scheme is especially useful for interval training that calls for frequent intensity shifts.

My first experience with a treadmill dial like this was a few years ago when I tried the original Peloton Tread. That machine carried a sky-high price, so seeing a similar control system on a much more affordable treadmill is a major plus.

The T6 also offers a 20-inch by 60-inch cushioning running belt, a top speed of 12 mph, motor-controlled incline up to 15%, a three-speed fan, and a foldable deck. Solid basics for a home treadmill, rather than padding out the package with a bigger screen.

Wrap-up

Overall, I highly recommend the BowFlex T6 treadmill for anyone looking to build out a home gym on a budget. BowFlex sells pricier models with more advanced displays and larger running decks, but the T6 covers the important features well without piling on costs I don't need.

GymKit paired with Apple Watch is a great experience, and it recently expanded to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3. If you're using a Samsung Galaxy Watch, this treadmill supports that too.

Have you used Apple Watch with Apple GymKit before? Share your experience in the comments.
